---
title: "Residuals"
execute:
  enabled: true

The Provo regression line assigns each word position a fitted conditional mean. A [**residual**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is the observed response minus that fitted value, as defined below.

This page first computes the position-level discrepancies, then connects their algebraic constraints to the passage patterns that remain available for checking.

$$
e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
$$

A positive residual marks a position above the fitted line; a negative residual marks one below it. The residual is observable after fitting. It is not the unobserved population error $\varepsilon_i$.

## Computing the Provo regression residuals

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-residuals
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)

provo$fitted_mean_log_ffd <- fitted(fit)
provo$residual <-
  provo$mean_log_ffd - provo$fitted_mean_log_ffd

stopifnot(
  max(abs(provo$residual - residuals(fit))) < 1e-12,
  abs(sum(provo$residual)) < 1e-10
)

summary(provo$residual)
```

The first observed subtraction is:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-provo-residual
provo[1L, c(
  "position_id", "mean_log_ffd", "fitted_mean_log_ffd", "residual"
)]
```

This response remains a position-level mean over reader log FFDs, as defined in the [Provo dossier](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data). A residual plot can expose patterns across positions or passages, but it cannot diagnose listener heterogeneity after listener identifiers have been removed.

With an intercept, the normal equations include

$$
\frac{\partial\operatorname{SSE}}{\partial\beta_0}
=
-2\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0.
$$

At the OLS solution, this gives

$$
\sum_i e_i=0.
$$

The Provo regression residuals sum to `r format(sum(provo$residual), scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`. That algebraic property is not evidence that positive and negative discrepancies are equally plausible in every region of the predictor.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-data-and-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Observed Provo position summaries with the fitted line, followed by the same discrepancies on a residual scale."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
grid$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.2
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first-fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Provo regression residuals against fitted values. The blue curve is a descriptive loess smooth."
residual_opacity <- 0.25
ggplot(provo, aes(fitted_mean_log_ffd, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = residual_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(x = "Fitted mean log FFD", y = "Residual") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The smooth bends modestly rather than remaining perfectly horizontal. This pattern motivates a functional-form check; it does not by itself establish which alternative model is correct.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does a positive residual place an observation above the line?
2. Why must OLS residuals sum to zero when the model has an intercept?
3. Is a residual the same object as an error term?
4. What model restriction does curvature challenge?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Because $e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i$, a positive value means $y_i>\widehat y_i$ and the point lies above the fitted line. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The intercept normal equation sets the derivative with respect to $\beta_0$ to zero, which requires $\sum_i e_i=0$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. No. A residual is an observed post-fit discrepancy; an error term is an unobserved random quantity in the population model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Curvature challenges the restriction that the conditional mean is a straight line in modeled cloze surprisal. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](checking-linear-regression.qmd) turns residual patterns into explicit model checks.
